1925–2021 · Canada and United States

Albert Bandura

Canadian psychologist who showed that we learn by watching others. His Bobo doll experiment and his concept of self-efficacy made him one of the most cited psychologists in the world.

Biography

Albert Bandura was born in 1925 in Mundare, a small town in Alberta, Canada, the son of immigrants from Poland and Ukraine. His school had only two teachers for the whole of secondary education, so pupils had to learn largely on their own. He studied at the University of British Columbia and took his doctorate at the University of Iowa in 1952.

From 1953 he was a professor at Stanford University, where he spent the rest of his career. He was president of the American Psychological Association in 1974 and received the US National Medal of Science in 2016. He died in 2021, aged 95.

Questions he investigated

  • Can a behaviour be learnt just by watching it, without practising it or being rewarded?
  • Do children imitate the aggression they see?
  • Why do some people persist in the face of difficulty while others give up?

Contributions

In 1961, with Dorothea and Sheila Ross, he showed pre-school children an adult hitting an inflatable doll called Bobo, while other children watched an adult playing quietly. Afterwards, the first group far more often imitated the blows and even the adult's words. It was evidence of observational learning: we learn by watching others, with no need for direct reinforcement.

In 1977 he proposed the concept of self-efficacy: confidence in one's ability to do a particular thing. People with high self-efficacy set themselves more ambitious challenges, try harder and recover better from failure. His social cognitive theory sees behaviour as the result of continuous interaction between the person, their behaviour and their environment.

Collaborations, influences and disagreements

He started from the behaviourist tradition but added mental processes such as attention, memory and expectations, which Skinner's radical behaviourism set aside. With his first doctoral student, Richard Walters, he studied aggression in adolescents. His ideas have influenced education, public health and campaigns that use role models in television series to promote healthy behaviour.

A documented anecdote

Bandura said he came to psychology by chance. At university he shared a car with students who started very early, and he looked for a course to fill that first hour. The only one that fitted was Introductory Psychology.

Criticism, limits and reception

Critics have noted that the Bobo doll was designed precisely to be hit, so it is not certain the children were acting with real aggression, and that the experiment measured behaviour only immediately after observation. Even so, observational learning and self-efficacy are among the most widely used and best-supported concepts in psychology.

References

  1. Bandura, A., Ross, D. y Ross, S. A. (1961). Transmission of aggression through imitation of aggressive models. Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology, 63(3), 575–582.
  2. Bandura, A. (1977). Self-efficacy: toward a unifying theory of behavioral change. Psychological Review, 84(2), 191–215.
  3. Bandura, A. (1986). Social foundations of thought and action: A social cognitive theory. Englewood Cliffs, NJ: Prentice-Hall.
